latin.54: Sequitur ratio quarta. Scopus Apostoli non patitur ut ita vertantur; coepit enim Apostolus vers. 12. comparationem inter Christum & Adamum instituere eo modo, ut affirmaret per unum hominem peccatum introiisse, & per peccatum mortem, adeo ut mors in omnes homines pervagata sit. Quia vero mirum videri potuit, tantam fuisse in unius hominis uno peccato vim atque efficacitatem, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, ne quis indigne quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, addit, id mirum videri non debere, cum omnes peccaverint. Ut igitur Adam in mortem incidit, quia peccavit; sic & omnes pariter in mortem incidunt, quia omnes peccaverunt.
latin.55: Quid reponit vir doctus? Primo, inquit, notetur respondentis confessio: Nam dum agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per unum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse unum unius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum, eadem ratione omnia illa argumenta confutat & convellit, quibus supra moliebatur alius confirmare, hic peccati nomine non ipsius Adami peccatum, sed nostram internam & originalem corruptionem tantum intelligendam esse. Ita-ne, omnia illa argumenta confutat & convellit? Possunt-ne unius simplici affirmatione, alterius argumenta & multa, & valida, & diu post illam affirmationem excogitata & proposita confutari & convelli? Si est ita, nullum est argumentum usque adeo necessarium, & demonstrativum, quod non possit ea ratione facillime confutari & convelli. Argumenta autem illa, quia sunt posterioris manuscripti, quam sint valida & invicta, tum fiet manifestum, cum instituetur manuscripti illius cum libro D. Gar. comparatio.
latin.56: Quid vero dices, candide Lector, si id non confitetur doctissimus autor illius rationis, quod hic confiteri dicitur? Certe non agnoscit peccatum illud, quod per unum hominem introiisse dicitur, esse unum unius hominis, nempe Adami peccatum: id non sentit: id neque totidem verbis dixit, neque aequipollentibus. Dixit tantum in uno unius peccato tantam fuisse vim, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret: sed non dixit illud unum unius peccatum idem numero in omnes homines ingressum esse, & proxime mortem invexisse. Nempe peccatum quod introiit in mundum est unius peccati unius hominis effectum, & per unum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum & mors vi unius peccati, quod sese propagatione naturali diffudit, & multiplicavit, & cum natura humana, cui inhaeret, propagavit. Itaque totam hominum multitudinem morti addixit sui in omnes homines propagatione, ac secundum numerum multiplicatione. Haec est praestantissimi illius viri mens, neque sibi, neque Placeo contradicentis.
latin.57: Haec prima fuit D. G. responsio. 2. Ad dubium, inquit, quod emergere potuit in lectorum animis, nulla esset plane Apostoli responsio legitima, si talem daret, qualem vult Vir Doctus. Dubium enim hoc est, quomodo tanta sit vis in uno unius Adami peccato, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addicat. Responsio dicitur esse, id inde fieri, quod omnes peccaverint in sua propria persona. Hoc vero ludere est, non dubio satisfacere. Nam haec quidem ratio esse potest, propter quam morti omnes addicantur, quia omnes peccarunt. Sed hic non quaeritur, quare omnes morti addicantur, verum hoc potius, cur in uno unius Adami peccato tanta vis sit, ut hunc effectum producat, nempe mortem. Responsio igitur debet agere de peccato illo Adami, non de nostro uniuscujusque, de quo nihil dictum fuerat in dubio proposito. Itaque ut apposita sit responsio, necessarium est, ut illud ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, interpretemur de peccato ipsius Adami, quod omnes morti addicat, propterea quod ejus reatus in omnes descendit, sive quia propter imputationem commune sit omnibus. Hoc ita clarum est & evidens, ut hic oporteat valde festinasse disputatorem. Festinavit quidem fortasse autor hujus rationis, sed non nimis: optime enim disputat. Sed an festinaverit D. G. nescio, illud certe mihi constat, eum hic, ut alibi passim, haud recte disputare.
latin.58: Non ludit, sed revera dubio satisfacit Responsio. Duobus enim modis in unius hominis uno peccato tantam vim fuisse, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, intelligi poterat, uno, si ponatur, quod facit hoc loco D. G. Deum toti hominum multitudini unum illud unius hominis peccatum immediate imputasse, atque ob illud imputatum eam morti addixisse. Altero, si intelligatur, peccatum illud sese naturali quodam contagio, ab uno homine in alios omnes propagasse & multiplicasse, atque ita, quoniam omnes peccaverunt, morti addictos fuisse. Apostolus ne Lector priorem modum cogitans, indigne quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, posteriorem docet, affirmans omnes homines morti fuisse addictos, non quia unus tantum peccavit, sed quia omnes peccaverunt; non proxime ob unius unum peccatum, sed ob suum quisque sibi insitum, ab illo uno propagatum, quae propagatio vocibus ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ita, non minus ad peccatum quam ad mortem pertinentibus, satis innuitur. Audi, quaeso humanissime Lector, Calvinum, a cujus doctrina recedant necesse est qui nos innovatae doctrinae accusant, Comm. in Rom. 5. 12. Observa quem hic ponat ordinem. Peccatum enim praecessisse dicit: ex eo sequutam esse mortem. Sunt enim qui contendunt, nos ita peccato Adae esse perditos ac si nulla nostra culpa periremus, ideo tantum quasi ille nobis peccasset. (Vix potuit clarius imputatio antecedens describi, quam sequi putantur mors animae, id est, corruptio haereditaria, & mors corporis ac aeterna, tanquam poenae proprie dictae.) Atqui diserte affirmat Paulus, in omnes propagatum esse peccatum, qui ejus poenam luunt. Atque id deinde propius urget, quum rationem assignat paulo post, cur omnis Adae posteritas subjaceat mortis imperio. Nempe, inquit, quoniam omnes peccavimus. Porro istud peccare, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Illa enim naturalis pravitas quam e matris utero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram Domino, & ejus ultionem meretur. Atque hoc est peccatum quod vocant Originale. Et paulo post, Peccavimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti sumus. Et iterum, Sequitur ergo pravitatem nobis ingenitam, & haereditariam notari. Nihil potuit dici clarius & disertius. Gratulatur sibi Placeus cum videt per latus suum peti Calvinum, seque cum eo pariter oppugnari, & desertae antiquae doctrinae, aut potius eam deserantium vices luget. Notetur hic rursus nova, &, ut mihi quidem videtur, Deo injuriosa doctrina, peccatum Adami propter imputationem commune fieri omnibus. Quod igitur commune est omnibus id non vi aut contagio aut naturali propagationi illius peccati ascribendum est, sed Deo, cui libuit imputando facere omnibus commune, quod alioqui commune non fuisset. Unde igitur nostra perditio, nisi ex Deo, qui nos fecit peccatores alienum peccatum efficiendo nostrum? Et cur peccatum illud nobis imputavit, & fecit nostrum, nosque peccatores? Nulla causa affertur, aut afferri potest, nisi quia ita ei libuit. Non excitatur conscientia tua, pie Lector? non refugit talem doctrinam? non exhorrescit? Sed pergamus.

pass_a.54: Next comes the fourth argument. Placeus says the Apostle's purpose will not bear the wording being twisted as Garissoles twists it. At Romans 5:12 Paul started a Christ–Adam comparison precisely so he could affirm entry of sin through one man and of death through sin, with the result that death ranged through the whole human race. The sheer force of one man's single sin in condemning the entire multitude could look astonishing; to keep anyone from thinking ill of God, Paul adds that astonishment is unnecessary because everyone has sinned. Adam entered death for his own sinning; equally, everyone enters death because everyone has sinned.
pass_a.55: Garissoles's first counter: note what the respondent (Placeus) allegedly concedes. Once Placeus grants that the sin said to enter through one man is Adam's single personal sin, Garissoles claims that same grant knocks down every earlier argument meant to show that 'sin' here means only our internal original corruption rather than Adam's own act. Placeus rejects the claim. One speaker's bare yes cannot overturn another writer's many solid proofs that were framed long after that yes. If that method worked, no necessary or demonstrative proof could survive. Those proofs live in a later manuscript; their strength will show when that manuscript is set beside Doctor Garissoles's book.
pass_a.56: Placeus turns to the candid reader: what if the author of the fourth argument never made the confession Garissoles attributes to him? He does not acknowledge, hold, or state—either in identical wording or in equivalents—that the entering sin is Adam's one sin in the charged sense. All he said was that one man's one sin carried force enough to doom the whole human multitude. He never said that numerically identical act walked into every person and immediately dragged death with it. What entered the world is the effect of that one sin; sin and death came through one man by the power of that sin as it spread, multiplied, and traveled with the human nature to which it clings. Condemnation of the multitude follows from that propagation into all and from multiplication by headcount. That reading is the excellent man's mind and contradicts neither himself nor Placeus.
pass_a.57: Garissoles's first reply ends there. His second targets the doubt readers might feel. He says Paul would have no lawful answer if Paul answered as Placeus wants. The doubt is how Adam's one sin can doom everyone. The answer Garissoles rejects is: because each person sinned in his own person. Placeus calls that playfulness, not a real reply. Personal sinning can explain why people are doomed; it does not explain why Adam's one act has the force to produce death. A fitting reply must talk about Adam's sin, not about each person's sin—which the posed doubt never mentioned. So Garissoles requires reading ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον as Adam's own sin whose guilt comes down on all, or which imputation makes common to all. He thinks this so obvious that Placeus must have rushed. Placeus answers that the fourth argument's author may have moved quickly but not too quickly—he argues well— while Garissoles, here as often, argues badly.
pass_a.58: Placeus insists the answer is serious and does meet the doubt. The claim that one man's one sin doomed the multitude admits two readings. Reading one (Garissoles's here): God immediately imputed that one sin to the whole multitude and doomed them for the imputed act. Reading two: the sin spread by natural contagion from one into all, multiplied, and so—because all had sinned—all were doomed. To keep readers from the first reading and from unworthy thoughts about God, Paul teaches the second: doom came because all sinned, not because only one did; each suffers for his own implanted sin transmitted from that one, not immediately for the single remote act. The ἐφ᾽ ᾧ wording itself hints at that transmission and touches sin no less than death. Placeus then cites Calvin's Romans 5:12 commentary—opponents who call Placeus novel must abandon Calvin. Calvin's order: sin first, death after. Some say we perish by Adam's sin with no fault of our own, as if he alone sinned for us; Placeus notes that that is almost a clear sketch of antecedent imputation, with soul-death (hereditary corruption) and bodily plus eternal death treated as proper punishments. But Paul states sin was propagated to all who bear its penalty, and presses the reason all Adam's line lies under death: we all sinned. That sinning means being corrupted and spoiled. The innate depravity brought from the womb is already sin before God and merits vengeance—original sin— even before it quickly yields fruit. Later Calvin lines: we all sinned because natural corruption fills us all; therefore inborn hereditary depravity is what is marked. Nothing could be clearer. Placeus is glad when the blow aimed at him also hits Calvin, and he grieves for the abandoned older teaching—or for those abandoning it. He flags again the new claim—injurious to God, in his view—that Adam's sin becomes everyone's only by imputation. Commonality is then blamed not on the sin's force, contagion, or natural spread, but on God, who by imputing chose to make common what otherwise would not be. Then our ruin would come from God making us sinners by turning another's sin into ours, with no reason except divine pleasure. Placeus asks whether a pious conscience is not stirred, recoiling, and horrified. Then: but let us proceed.

54: The fourth reason follows. The Apostle's scope will not allow them to be turned that way; for the Apostle began at verse 12 (Romans 5:12) to institute a comparison between Christ and Adam in such a manner as to affirm that through one man sin entered, and through sin death, so that death spread abroad upon all men. But because it could seem strange that there was so great force and efficacy in one man's one sin that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death, lest anyone should suspect anything unworthy of God, he adds that this ought not to seem strange, since all have sinned. As therefore Adam fell into death because he sinned, so also all alike fall into death because all have sinned.
55: What does the learned man reply? "First," he says, "let the respondent's confession be noted: for while he acknowledges that that sin which is said to have entered through one man is one sin of one man, namely Adam's, by the same reason he confutes and overthrows all those arguments by which another above was striving to confirm that here by the name of sin not Adam's own sin, but only our inward and original corruption, is to be understood." Does he so confute and overthrow all those arguments? Can another's arguments — many, and strong, and long after that affirmation devised and proposed — be confuted and overthrown by one man's simple affirmation? If it is so, there is no argument so necessary and demonstrative that it cannot by that reason be most easily confuted and overthrown. But those arguments, because they belong to a later manuscript, how valid and invincible they are will then become plain when a comparison of that manuscript with Doctor Garissoles's book is instituted.
56: But what will you say, candid reader, if the most learned author of that reason does not confess what he is here said to confess? Certainly he does not acknowledge that that sin which is said to have entered through one man is one sin of one man, namely Adam's: he does not hold that; he said it neither in so many words nor in equivalent ones. He said only that in one man's one sin there was such force that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death; but he did not say that that one sin of one man entered into all men as the same in number, and brought death in immediately. Namely, the sin that entered into the world is the effect of one sin of one man; and through one man sin entered into the world, and death by the force of one sin, which diffused and multiplied itself by natural propagation, and propagated with the human nature in which it inheres. Therefore it sentenced the whole multitude of men to death by its propagation into all men, and by multiplication according to number. This is that most excellent man's mind, contradicting neither himself nor Placeus.
57: This was Doctor Garissoles's first response. 2. "As to the doubt," he says, "which could arise in readers' minds, there would plainly be no legitimate response of the Apostle if he gave such a one as the learned man wants. For this is the doubt: how there is so great force in one sin of one Adam that it sentences the whole multitude of men to death. The response is said to be that this comes about thence, that all have sinned in their own person. But this is to play, not to satisfy the doubt. For this reason can indeed be why all are sentenced to death, because all have sinned. But here it is not asked why all are sentenced to death, but rather this: why in one sin of one Adam there is so great force that it produces this effect, namely death. The response therefore ought to deal with that sin of Adam, not with each of ours, about which nothing had been said in the doubt proposed. Therefore, for the response to be fitting, it is necessary that we interpret ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον of Adam's own sin, which sentences all to death because its reatus descends upon all, or because through imputation it becomes common to all. This is so clear and evident that here the disputant must have been in a great hurry." The author of this reason may perhaps have hurried, but not too much: for he disputes excellently. But whether Doctor Garissoles hurried, I do not know; this much is certain to me, that he here, as elsewhere throughout, does not dispute rightly.
58: The response does not play, but truly satisfies the doubt. For in two ways it could be understood that there was such force in one man's one sin that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death: in one way, if it is supposed — which Doctor Garissoles does in this place — that God immediately imputed that one sin of one man to the whole multitude of men, and for that imputed sin sentenced it to death. In the other, if it is understood that that sin propagated and multiplied itself by a certain natural contagion from one man into all others, and so, since all have sinned, they were sentenced to death. The Apostle, lest the reader thinking the former way should suspect anything unworthy of God, teaches the latter, affirming that all men were sentenced to death not because one alone sinned, but because all have sinned; not immediately on account of one man's one sin, but on account of each man's own implanted in him, propagated from that one — which propagation is sufficiently hinted by the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, pertaining no less to sin than to death. Hear, I ask, most kindly reader, Calvin, from whose doctrine those who accuse us of innovated doctrine must of necessity withdraw — Commentary on Romans 5:12. Observe what order he sets here. For he says that sin preceded: from it death followed. For there are those who contend that we are so lost by Adam's sin as if we perished by no fault of our own, only because he had as it were sinned for us. (Antecedent imputation could scarcely be described more clearly than as that which death of the soul — that is, hereditary corruption — and death of the body and eternal death are thought to follow, as punishments properly so called.) And yet Paul expressly affirms that sin has been propagated to all who undergo its punishment. And then he presses that more closely when a little later he assigns the reason why all Adam's posterity lies under the empire of death. Namely, he says, because we have all sinned. Further, that 'to sin' is to be corrupted and spoiled. For that natural depravity which we bring from the mother's womb, even if it does not so quickly put forth its fruits, is yet sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And this is the sin which they call Original. And a little later: We have therefore all sinned, because we are all imbued with natural corruption. And again: It follows therefore that depravity inborn and hereditary in us is marked. Nothing could be said more clearly and expressly. Placeus congratulates himself when he sees Calvin struck through his side, and himself attacked together with him, and mourns the lot of the deserted ancient doctrine, or rather of those deserting it. Let it be noted here again the new doctrine — and, as it seems to me, injurious to God — that Adam's sin becomes common to all because of imputation. What therefore is common to all is to be ascribed not to the force or contagion or natural propagation of that sin, but to God, to whom it pleased by imputing to make common to all what otherwise would not have been common. Whence then our perdition, if not from God, who made us sinners by making another's sin ours? And why did he impute that sin to us, and make it ours, and us sinners? No cause is brought, or can be brought, except that it so pleased him. Is your conscience not stirred, pious reader? Does it not shrink from such a doctrine? Does it not shudder? But let us go on.
